title: Judith
subtitle: a widow, a besieged town, and a God who saves by a woman's hand
lead: Judith tells how a vast army threatened the Jews soon after their return from exile. Nebuchadnezzar, called here "king of the Assyrians" in Nineveh, defeats a Median king named Arphaxad and sends his general Holofernes west to punish every nation that refused to help him and to make the world worship the king alone. Judea stands in his way, and the small hill town of Bethulia blocks the passes to Jerusalem. Holofernes cuts off its water. After 34 days the people beg their leaders to surrender, and the leaders promise to give in after five more days. Then Judith, a rich, devout and beautiful widow, rebukes them for putting God to the test. She prays, dresses in her finest clothes, walks into the enemy camp with her maid, wins the general's trust with clever words, and on the fourth night cuts off his head while he lies drunk. The army flees, Israel praises her, and she leads the women in a song of victory. It has 16 chapters and 340 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church and the Orthodox churches (Eastern and Oriental, including the Ethiopian and Eritrean) include Judith in their Old Testament; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, "of the second canon." Protestants place it among the Apocrypha: Lutheran and Anglican Bibles long printed it between the Testaments to be read for example of life, but not to set doctrine, and Reformed and Baptist confessions give it no authority. It is not in the Jewish Bible, and no copy was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, though medieval Jews retold the story in Hebrew and linked it with Hanukkah. Most scholars read it as a deliberately unhistorical story written in Hebrew in Judea around 150–100 BC.
facts: The Catholic Church (defined at Trent, 1546), the Eastern Orthodox churches, the Oriental Orthodox churches and the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches. Among the Apocrypha for Lutherans and Anglicans (read, not used for doctrine). Not Scripture for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.
Unknown. The book never names its writer. Most scholars think of a devout Jew of Judea, writing long after the times in which the story is set.

Most scholars: about 150–100 BC, under the Hasmonean rulers who came after the Maccabees. A few place the story's core in the Persian period (400s–300s BC). The latest possible date is about AD 96, when 1 Clement praises Judith.

The book's own setting: the 18th year of Nebuchadnezzar, "king of the Assyrians" in Nineveh (2:1), soon after the Jews had returned from exile and rededicated the Temple (4:3). The action takes place in the hills of Samaria, at Bethulia, a town otherwise unknown, near Dothan and the valley of Esdraelon (4:6).
Probably Judea, since the writer centers everything on Jerusalem and its Temple and knows the land of Israel better than the East
Probably Hebrew, now lost. The Greek reads like a close translation of Hebrew. Jerome translated from a copy in "Chaldean" (Aramaic), and Origen was told the Jews had no Hebrew Judith.

Greek (Codex Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus, 300s–400s AD, and Codex Sinaiticus; groups of later minuscule manuscripts); the Old Latin; Jerome's Latin Vulgate; Syriac and other translations made from the Greek; medieval Hebrew retellings, which are later versions, not the original. No copy was found at Qumran.
A short story or novella of deliverance, with speeches (5; 8; 11), a prayer (9) and a victory song (16)
16 chapters, 340 verses (in this site's numbering, which follows the Greek)
authorship: For many centuries Catholic and Orthodox readers took Judith as a true account. The book never names its author, and tradition fixed none. Augustine placed its events in the time after the exile, under the Persians (City of God 18.26). Catholic scholars of the 1700s–1800s defended the history point by point. As Hugh Pope's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) reports, Augustin Calmet took Nebuchadnezzar to be the Babylonian king and Arphaxad to be Phraortes of Media, while Fulcran Vigouroux identified Nebuchadnezzar with the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal and set the story in the time of Manasseh's captivity (2 Chronicles 33:11). Pope's article puts the geographical errors down to translators and copyists. Some Catholic and Orthodox readers still take the story as history.

Most scholars, including most Catholic scholars today, read Judith as an edifying story by an unknown Jewish writer of about 150–100 BC. The writer mixes empires and centuries on purpose (see "How reliable is it?"): the enemy is a composite of every king who ever threatened Israel, and the heroine's name, Judith, means "Jewish woman." Carey Moore and Deborah Gera both take this view; J. E. Bruns in the New Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the book resists historical dating and that Bethulia may be a symbolic name.

Some scholars think the story grew from real events of the Persian period. The Encyclopaedia Judaica article by Yehoshua Grintz and Bathja Bayer notes that the book has plainly Persian names (Holofernes, Bagoas), points to a Cappadocian prince named Holofernes who fought in Egypt for the Persian king Artaxerxes III in 352 BC, and finds the story's historical core there, while judging the book itself more probably a Hasmonean historical novel. It also reports a view that the book was written at the end of the Persian period.

audience.to: Most scholars think of Jews in Judea under the Hasmonean high priests and kings, the heirs of the Maccabees, in the later 100s BC. They remembered how Antiochus IV had tried to stamp out their religion (167–164 BC) and how a small, faithful people had won. Their rulers were now pushing north into Samaria and Galilee, where Bethulia is set. The book's world of a high priest and a council of elders ruling from Jerusalem (4:8; 15:8) fits their time, not the time of Nebuchadnezzar. Readers who knew the Scriptures would catch at once that "Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians" is a joke at history's expense, a picture of every great enemy rolled into one.
audience.why: The writer wanted to show that God saves his people when they trust him and keep his law, even against the greatest power on earth, and that he does it through the weak: "by a woman's hand" (9:10; 13:15; 16:5). Nebuchadnezzar demands to be worshiped as the only god (3:8; 6:2); the book answers that the God of Israel alone is God. Its heroine models the piety its readers prized: prayer, fasting, widowhood kept with honor, the food laws kept even in the enemy's tent (12:1–4), and a faith that does not set deadlines for God (8:11–17). Its foreign convert Achior shows that outsiders who see what God has done may join Israel (14:10). Knowing the readers changes the reading. Judith is not a chronicle of an Assyrian war. It is a story about faith under threat, told to a people who had just lived through one.
views: Most scholars, such as Moore and Nickelsburg, date the book to about 150–100 BC and read it as a celebration of the Maccabean spirit: a faithful few, a threatened Temple, and an enemy's head displayed on the wall (14:1), as Judas Maccabeus displayed Nicanor's (1 Maccabees 7:47).

Some have argued that the book was written at the end of the Persian period, in the 300s BC, since it has Persian names and a Temple newly rebuilt (4:3), as the Encyclopaedia Judaica reports. Most scholars still prefer a Hasmonean date, because the council of elders ruling with the high priest in Jerusalem (4:8) and the mood of a holy war won by the faithful fit the age after the Maccabees.
A story for the whole people

Many readers note that the heroine's name means "Jewish woman" and that her town may be a symbol. On this reading she stands for the people itself, weak and widowed, who triumph when they trust God. Luther already read the book this way in 1534: he said the allegory "strikes my fancy" and thought the poet had put in the errors of time and name on purpose.

For the churches that read it as Scripture, the readers include the church, which hears in Judith a call to trust God in danger and, in Catholic tradition, sees in her a figure of Mary and of the church overcoming evil.

outline: Nebuchadnezzar defeats Arphaxad of Media and vows revenge on the western nations that refused to help him
Holofernes' campaign: the nations surrender, their shrines are destroyed, and the king is to be worshiped as god
Judea, newly returned from exile, fortifies the passes and cries to God in sackcloth
Achior the Ammonite tells Holofernes Israel's history and warns him; he is handed over to Bethulia
The siege of Bethulia: the springs are seized, the people despair, and the leaders promise to surrender in five days
Judith the widow: her piety, her rebuke of the elders, and her secret plan
Judith's prayer at the hour of the evening incense
Judith dresses in her finest and goes down to the Assyrian camp
Three days in the camp: Judith keeps the food laws and prays; the banquet
Judith beheads Holofernes and returns to Bethulia with his head
Achior believes and is circumcised; the head on the wall; panic in the Assyrian camp
The rout of the army, the plunder, and the praise of Judith by the high priest and the women of Israel
Offerings in Jerusalem; Judith's long life, her refusal to remarry, and her death

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Judith among the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament, defined as Scripture at the Council of Trent (1546), and its liturgy applies the praises of Judith to Mary.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches read Judith in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint, among the books many Eastern teachers call "worthy to be read" (anagignoskomena).

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Judith among the Apocrypha: once printed between the Testaments to be read for example of life, but not to establish doctrine (Article VI), and given no authority by Reformed churches (Westminster Confession 1.3).

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read Judith as a deliberately unhistorical tale from the Maccabean or Hasmonean age (about 150–100 BC), mixing eras and empires to show how God saves through the weak.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Judith is not in the Jewish Bible, but medieval Jews retold her story in Hebrew and linked it with Hanukkah, and her courage became part of Jewish lore and art.

sections.b:
Read it first as a story, and notice how it is built. The first seven chapters are all about power: a world empire, an army of thousands, a general who asks, "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" (6:2). Judith does not appear until chapter 8. The last nine chapters are all about one woman, and they turn every boast of the first half upside down. The general who would cut off Israel's head loses his own (13:8).

Then watch for irony. Judith speaks to Holofernes in words that are true in a way he cannot see: she calls him "my lord" and speaks of what God will accomplish "with you" (11:5–6), and she promises that not a dog will so much as mutter at him (11:19). The reader knows what she means; he does not. Much of the book's power, and much of the moral debate about it, comes from this double speech.

Read it beside the stories it echoes: Jael killing Sisera in her tent and Deborah's song (Judges 4–5), David taking Goliath's head (1 Samuel 17:51–54), Simeon's revenge for Dinah, which Judith praises in her prayer (9:2–4; Genesis 34), and Miriam's song at the sea (Exodus 15:20–21). The notes mark where Judith draws on the Hebrew Bible, where the New Testament may echo it, and where it goes beyond or differs from the 66 books.

The Plain English is translated for this site from the Greek, as printed by H. B. Swete (1907), who prints the text of Codex Vaticanus and gives the readings of Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Sinaiticus in his notes. The variant notes report where those manuscripts, the later Greek groups, the Old Latin and Jerome's Latin Vulgate differ in ways that matter.

Jerome's Vulgate, which the Douay-Rheims Bible translates, is about a fifth shorter than the Greek and numbers its verses differently: Uzziah's blessing of Judith is 13:18 in the Greek but 13:23 in the Vulgate, and the Vulgate alone ends with a note that the Jews kept the day of the victory as a feast (Vulgate 16:31). The King James Version's Apocrypha, which follows the Greek, and the Douay-Rheims were used only to check the sense. Names use the usual English forms (Judith, Holofernes, Nebuchadnezzar, Arphaxad, Achior, Uzziah, Bethulia, Joakim, Bagoas), with the Greek in a note the first time where it differs.

Who is God? The question runs through the whole book. The king sends his army so that every nation will call on him as god (3:8); Achior says Israel is safe as long as it does not sin against its God (5:17–21); Holofernes answers, "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" (6:2). Judith's prayer gives the book's answer: God's strength does not lie in numbers, for he is "the God of the lowly," "the helper of the least, the protector of the weak" (9:11).

Do not test God. When the leaders of Bethulia promise to surrender unless God helps within five days, Judith tells them they have no right to set terms for God: no one can search out his mind (8:11–17). Instead the people should thank God, who tests them as he tested Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:25–27).

By a woman's hand. Judith prays that God will strike the enemy "by a woman's hand" (9:10), and the phrase returns at the climax (13:15) and in her song (16:5). In the ancient world a widow was among the weakest of people; here she is the one through whom God saves, while the town's men sit and wait.

Faithfulness in the details. Judith fasts and prays (8:5–6), keeps the food laws in the enemy's tent (12:1–4), bathes and prays each night (12:7–8), and lives as a widow to the end (16:22). The book shows a holiness made of daily faithfulness, not only of one heroic act.

The outsider who believes. Achior the Ammonite tells the truth about Israel's God, suffers for it, and at the end believes and is circumcised (14:10), though the Law of Moses barred Ammonites from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). The chapter pages discuss that tension.

Judith is drawn from the women and heroes of Israel's past. Like Jael she is alone with an enemy general in a tent and kills him while he lies helpless (Judges 4:17–22; Judges 5:24–27), though Jael's tent was her own and Judith is taken into Holofernes' (13:1–2), and Uzziah's blessing of her (13:18) recalls Deborah's blessing of Jael, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24). Like Deborah she leads Israel's song of victory (16:1–17; Judges 5). Like Miriam she leads the women with music (15:12–16:1; Exodus 15:20–21). Like David she goes out alone against a mighty enemy and brings back his head (1 Samuel 17:51–54). Like Esther she uses beauty and banquets in a foreign court to save her people, and like Esther in the Greek additions (Addition C, Esther 14:17 in the KJV Apocrypha) and Daniel she keeps herself from Gentile food (12:2; Daniel 1:8). She traces her family to Simeon, who avenged his sister Dinah: her genealogy runs through Salamiel son of Sarasadai, the leader of Simeon's tribe in Numbers 1:6 (8:1), and she calls Simeon her ancestor (9:2–4; Genesis 34). Her very name, the feminine of Hebrew Yehudi, "Jew," makes her the Jewish people in one person.

sections.h: Judith in worship, art and Jewish memory
sections.b:
In Catholic worship. The Latin church has long applied Judith's praises to Mary. The Gradual of the Mass of the Immaculate Conception in the Roman Missal used until 1970 sings Uzziah's blessing (Vulgate 13:23), with "Virgin Mary" in place of "daughter," and then the people's praise, "You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel, you are the honor of our people" (Vulgate 15:10). In the Liturgy of the Hours the same words are an antiphon of Evening Prayer on that feast, and a canticle from Judith's song (16:2–3a, 13–15 in the breviary's numbering; 16:1–2a, 13–15 in this site's) is sung at Morning Prayer on Wednesday of Week I. In the lectionary of the United States, Judith 13:18–19 is the responsorial psalm for the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Medieval picture books of salvation, such as the Speculum humanae salvationis, set Judith beheading Holofernes beside Mary overcoming the devil.

In the Orthodox churches Judith is part of the Old Testament, read from the Septuagint; we have found no source for regular readings from Judith in the Byzantine services.

In Jewish memory. Judith is not in the Jewish Bible, but medieval Jews retold her story in Hebrew, often setting it in the Maccabean war and reading it at Hanukkah. Rashi explained the Talmud's saying that women "too were part of the miracle" of Hanukkah (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 23a) by a story of a woman who saved Israel, without naming her; the Tosafot (on Megillah 4a) named her Judith; and Moses Isserles (the Rema) recorded the custom of eating cheese on Hanukkah because of the milk that Judith gave the enemy.

In art. From Donatello's bronze in Florence to the paintings of Caravaggio and Artemisia Gentileschi, Judith with the head of Holofernes became one of the most painted scenes in Western art, read in turn as civic liberty, the virtue of chastity, and, by some modern readers, female strength.

• Judith (Greek Ioudeith, Hebrew Yehudit), "Jewish woman" or "woman of Judah," daughter of Merari, widow of Manasseh.
  • Holofernes (Greek Olophernēs), the commander of the army. The name is Persian, not Assyrian.
  • Bagoas (12:11), the eunuch in charge of Holofernes' household, also a Persian name.
  • Nebuchadnezzar (Greek Nabouchodonosor), in history king of Babylon (605–562 BC), here the king "who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (1:1) and "king of the Assyrians" (2:1).
  • Arphaxad, who "ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana" (1:1), a king unknown to history.
  • Achior, "leader of all the Ammonites" (5:5), whose name may mean "brother of light."
  • Bethulia (Greek Baityloua, in some places Betyloua), the besieged town, otherwise unknown. The name may echo Hebrew betulah, "virgin," or beth-El, "house of God."
  • Uzziah (Greek Ozias), chief magistrate of Bethulia; Joakim, the high priest in Jerusalem (4:6; 15:8).
  • Hagiographa, "holy writings," the third part of the Hebrew Bible, where Jerome says the Jews of his day placed Judith.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the eighteenth year undone
spec.body: Holofernes' campaign is launched in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year (2:1). In the Bible that is the year of the last siege of Jerusalem, when the real Nebuchadnezzar carried off people from the city (Jeremiah 32:1; Jeremiah 52:29); the Temple burned the next year (2 Kings 25:8–9). The writer may be retelling Israel's worst disaster with a different ending: the same king, the same moment, the same threat to the Temple, but this time the people repent and pray (4:9–15), a widow acts, and the sanctuary is saved (16:18–20). Scholars have often noted that the book mixes eras on purpose, and commentators have connected the eighteenth year with the fall of Jerusalem; reading the whole book as a deliberate reversal of 587 BC is my own suggestion.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Achior's true words become Judith's bait
spec.body: Achior tells Holofernes the truth: Israel cannot be beaten unless it sins against its God (5:17–21). Judith later tells Holofernes that the people are about to sin by eating food set apart for God, so God will hand them over (11:10–15). Commentators note that she takes up Achior's theology. My suggestion is that the book does this to make a point about that theology itself. The rule is true, and the story proves it, but it is not a lever: the elders tried to use it to force God's hand with a deadline (8:11–17), and Holofernes tries to use it to time his attack. Only Judith, who refuses to bargain with God, sees how it will really work.

views: Yes. Judith is one of the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament. It was on the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) and of Pope Innocent I (405), and the Council of Florence (1442) named it. The Council of Trent (1546) defined the whole list, Judith included, as sacred and canonical, with an anathema on anyone who rejects it, and the Catechism (120) lists it. Catholics call it "deuterocanonical," a word for books received later or after debate, not less inspired.

Yes, in the Old Testament, though Orthodox teachers explain its rank in two ways. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named Judith among the "genuine parts of Scripture." Athanasius (367) had listed it among books "to be read" by those preparing for baptism, not in the canon, and Philaret's catechism (1839) follows his 22-book count. Kallistos Ware writes that most Orthodox scholars today hold these books are part of the Bible but stand on a lower footing.

Yes, by long use. The Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches read Judith in their Old Testament, in translations made from the Greek. They have held no council like Trent to define the list; their Bibles and teaching are the evidence, for example a Coptic diocese's page that lists Judith among the deuterocanonical books the Egyptian church received.
Yes. Judith is among the Old Testament books of the 81-book Bible of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches, in Ge'ez.

Not Scripture, but good to read. Luther's Bible of 1534 put Judith with the Apocrypha between the Testaments, as books not held equal to Holy Scripture yet useful and good to read. His preface to Judith says that if the events could be proved from reliable histories it would be "a noble and fine book" and "should properly be in the Bible," but that its names and times do not fit, so it may be a holy religious poem, an allegory of the Jewish people (Judith) overcoming the godless heathen (Holofernes). Lutheran confessions never fixed the canon; Martin Chemnitz taught that such books may not be used to prove doctrine.

Not canonical, but read. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "the Book of Judith" among the books that "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine," quoting Jerome. The King James Version printed it with the Apocrypha.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture." The Belgic Confession (article 6) names Judith among books the church may read for instruction where they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm any point of faith. Reformed writers such as Archibald Alexander added that Judith's lies and her praise of Simeon's massacre show the book is not from God.

No. The Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration, while still citing and esteeming some of these books; Judith is listed among them, though not singled out.
No. John Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) kept the Anglican list of canonical books but left out the paragraph that names the Apocrypha, so Judith has no place in Methodist doctrine.

No. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.2–3) lists the 66 books and nearly repeats Westminster: the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Most Baptists and other evangelicals read Judith, if at all, as Jewish literature from between the Testaments.

traditions.q: Must Judith's story have happened as told?
views: Not necessarily. The Church has made no ruling on Judith's genre known to us. Pius XII's Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) told interpreters to identify the literary forms the biblical writers used, and Dei Verbum (12) teaches that truth is expressed differently in history, prophecy, poetry and other kinds of writing. On that basis most Catholic scholars today read Judith as a story told to teach. Older Catholic writers, such as Hugh Pope in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), defended its history and blamed the difficulties on copyists, and some Catholics still do.

No ruling known to us. The Orthodox read Judith in church for its witness to faith and prayer, and many Orthodox teachers already give these books a lower rank than the Hebrew canon, so the question of genre weighs less.

No, and this is part of why it is not Scripture. Luther's preface says the names and times do not agree with history, and suggests it is a religious poem, written so that the Jewish people could see in Judith their own victory through faith.

Since it is not Scripture, nothing rests on it; its errors of history and geography are one proof that it is not inspired. Archibald Alexander (1826) set out the chronological problems as evidence against its authority.

canon.summary: Judith is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and of the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Ethiopian and Eritrean; Catholics call it deuterocanonical. Lutherans and Anglicans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. Augustine counted it in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13). It is on the list of the Council of Hippo (393), repeated at Carthage (397), and in Pope Innocent I's letter to Exsuperius (405). The Council of Florence (1442), in its decree of union with the Copts, listed it. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546) defined the list, Judith included, as sacred and canonical, and received all its books "with an equal affection of piety and reverence." The Catechism (120) names Judith among the books. For centuries the Catholic text was Jerome's shorter Vulgate; modern Catholic translations follow the Greek. The liturgy applies Judith's praises to Mary (see "Judith in worship, art and Jewish memory").

In the Old Testament, which the Orthodox read in the Greek of the Septuagint. Its rank has been explained in two ways. Athanasius (367) listed Judith among books "to be read" by those preparing for baptism, not among the canonical books, and the Russian catechism of Philaret (1839) follows his 22-book count. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering Protestant ideas, named Judith among the "genuine parts of Scripture." Kallistos Ware reports that most Orthodox scholars today treat these books as part of the Bible but on a lower footing than the rest; some Orthodox writers, as the Orthodox Church in America's answer does, simply call them canonical. Orthodox Bibles print it.

In their Old Testament by long use, in translations made from the Greek. These churches never held a council like Trent to define the list. A Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page lists Judith among the deuterocanonical books that the Egyptian church accepted and says they are found in the Coptic version. The Assyrian Church of the East is not covered here.
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches
Scripture, among the Old Testament books of the 81-book Bible, in a Ge'ez translation made from the Greek.

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (Latin 1563, English 1571) names "the Book of Judith" among the other books that, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it with the Apocrypha. Modern Anglican provinces differ in how much they read it.

Among the Apocrypha. Luther's complete Bible of 1534 gathered these books between the Testaments under a heading that called them books not held equal to Holy Scripture, yet useful and good to read. His preface to Judith (1534) doubts that it is history and suggests reading it as a holy poem, an allegory in which Judith is the Jewish people, Holofernes the godless heathen ruler and Bethulia, "a virgin," the faithful community. Lutheran confessions never fixed a canon; Martin Chemnitz (1565–73) taught that such books may not prove doctrine.

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 6) names Judith among the books the church may read and take instruction from as far as they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm faith. The Westminster Confession (1646) says the Apocrypha are "no part of the canon of the Scripture" and are not "to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings." Reformed writers gave moral reasons too: Archibald Alexander (1826) said Judith speaks almost nothing but falsehood to Holofernes and asks the God of truth to bless her deceit.

Not Scripture. The Global Anabaptist Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration, while Menno Simons and Dirk Philips often cited some of these books; it lists Judith among them but does not single it out.
Not Scripture. Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) took over the Anglican list of canonical books but dropped the paragraph naming the Apocrypha.

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) nearly repeats Westminster's words, calling the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Most evangelical churches hold the 66 books and read Judith, when they read it, as Jewish literature from between the Testaments, a view argued at length by Roger Beckwith and F. F. Bruce.

Not Scripture. Judith is not in the Hebrew Bible. Origen reported (about 240) that the Jews did not use Judith, and that, as he learned from Jews themselves, it was not even among their apocrypha in Hebrew. Jerome (about 405) said that the Jews read it among the Hagiographa but did not think it fit to settle disputed questions. No copy has been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. In the Middle Ages, Jewish writers retold the story in short Hebrew versions, often setting it in the Maccabean age, and linked it with Hanukkah: Rashi, the Tosafot and the Kol Bo connect Judith with the feast, and Moses Isserles records the custom of eating cheese on Hanukkah in her memory (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 670:2).

Widely read and usually treated as Scripture, with some doubts. The first Christian mention is in 1 Clement (about AD 96), which praises "the blessed Judith" who went out into the enemy camp for her people, so that the Lord handed Holofernes over "by the hand of a woman" (1 Clement 55.4–5). Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and Origen also cite it, as Hugh Pope reports. Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower, each in his own way: Athanasius (367) among books "to be read" by those newly joining the church; Rufinus (about 404) among the "ecclesiastical" books read in church but not used to confirm faith; Jerome among books the church reads for the building up of the people; Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) gave those preparing for baptism a 22-book list without Judith. The North African councils, Innocent I and Augustine counted it in the canon, though Augustine noted that the Jews were said not to have received it (City of God 18.26).

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b: Most scholars date Judith to about 150–100 BC, in the time of the Hasmonean rulers of Judea, the family of the Maccabees. The reasons: the book assumes a world after the exile, with the Temple rebuilt (4:3; 5:18–19); Jerusalem is ruled by a high priest with a council of elders, the gerousia (4:8; 15:8), as in the Hellenistic age; the story breathes the spirit of the Maccabean victories, down to the enemy's head hung on the wall (14:1; compare 1 Maccabees 7:47); and its setting in Samaria and the valley of Esdraelon fits a time when the Hasmoneans were expanding north. The latest possible date is about AD 96, when 1 Clement mentions Judith. A minority place the book, or at least its core, in the late Persian period because of its Persian names (Holofernes, Bagoas). Most think it was written in Judea, by a writer who knew the Scriptures and the Temple well and the eastern empires poorly.

No copy of Judith in Hebrew or Aramaic from ancient times survives, and none was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Yet nearly all scholars think it was first written in a Semitic language, most say Hebrew, because the Greek reads like a close, sometimes wooden translation: its sentences are chained with "and," it uses Hebrew idioms word for word, and some odd Greek phrases are best explained as a translator's misreading of a Hebrew word. Ancient testimony is mixed. Origen, about 240, wrote that the Jews did not use Judith and did not have it even among their apocrypha in Hebrew, as he learned from Jews themselves. Jerome, about 405, said he translated from a copy written "in Chaldean," that is, Aramaic, which may have been a later Aramaic version rather than the original. The medieval Hebrew retellings are not the original either: they are much shorter, change names and places, and seem to come from the Greek or Latin (see "Medieval Hebrew retellings").

The Greek survives in the great codices and in many later manuscripts, which scholars group in somewhat different ways. One count, as reported in the Zondervan Encyclopedia of the Bible after L. H. Brockington, finds four forms: (1) the great uncials, Codex Vaticanus (B) and Codex Alexandrinus (A) with Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ); (2) the minuscules 19 and 108, usually called the Lucianic or Antiochene text; (3) minuscule 58, close to the Old Latin and the Syriac; and (4) minuscules 106 and 107. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) and J. E. Bruns count three forms: the uncials together, 19 and 108, and 58. The Encyclopaedia Judaica counts four main forms too, but names them differently (A, B, 58 and 108). Unlike Tobit, Judith has no long and short forms: the differences are smaller, though many. Robert Hanhart's Göttingen edition (1979) is the standard critical text. Swete's edition, used for this site, prints Vaticanus and reports Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus in its notes.

The Old Latin (Vetus Latina), made in the early centuries from the Greek, survives in several forms that differ among themselves.

Jerome's Vulgate is a different kind of text. In his preface Jerome says that the Jews count Judith among the Hagiographa, whose authority "toward confirming those which have come into contention is judged less appropriate"; that, being written in Chaldean, it is counted among the histories; that "the Nicene Council" is found to have counted it "among the number of the Sacred Scriptures," and so he agreed to the bishops' request; and that he gave it "one short night's work," translating sense for sense and cutting out the "extremely faulty variety" of the many copies (all quoted from Kevin Edgecomb's translation). He ends by praising Judith as an example of chastity. The result is about a fifth shorter than the Greek, with its own wording and some additions: in the Vulgate Judith is praised for having "loved chastity" (Vulgate 15:11), and the book ends by saying the Jews kept the day of the victory as a holy day "from that time until this day" (Vulgate 16:31, Douay-Rheims). Jerome's Vulgate was the Catholic Judith for over a thousand years, and the Douay-Rheims (1609–10) translated it.

Jerome's remark that the Council of Nicaea (325) counted Judith among the Scriptures has puzzled readers ever since. The council's acts are lost; only its creed and twenty canons survive, and none of them lists the books of the Bible. Jerome's Latin says the synod "is read" (legitur, "is found written") to have done so, which tells us he relied on a document or report he does not name. Explanations differ. Hugh Pope (1910) says it is uncertain whether Jerome meant something said in the council's discussions or a set of spurious canons circulating under its name. The Catholic writer Jimmy Akin argues that records of the council now lost may have survived into Jerome's day, so that Nicaea may really have counted Judith among the Scriptures, and infers that it likely recognized other deuterocanonical books too, though he grants that the remark does not prove Nicaea dealt with the canon as a whole. Against this, no surviving document supports the report, and Jerome's own earlier prefaces (to Samuel and Kings, about 391; to the books of Solomon, about 398) had placed Judith outside the canon. What is certain is only what Jerome wrote, and that it moved him to translate the book.

From about the 900s on, Jews retold Judith in Hebrew. A short version found by Moses Gaster, which Hugh Pope dates to the 900s or 1000s, has an enemy named Seleucus attacking Jerusalem itself, with no Holofernes, Bethulia or Achior. Other versions, printed by Adolph Jellinek in his Bet ha-Midrasch, include one titled "The story of Judith, a midrash for Hanukkah," as the McClintock and Strong Cyclopaedia reports. In some of them Judith is a daughter of the high priest Yohanan, of the Maccabees' family, and the story is set in the Maccabean war. Medieval rabbis connected her with the feast: Rashi explained the Talmud's saying that women "too were part of the miracle" of Hanukkah (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 23a) by a woman who saved Israel, without naming her; the Tosafot (on Megillah 4a) named her Judith; the Kol Bo tells how she fed the enemy cheese before cutting off his head; and Moses Isserles (the Rema) records the custom of eating cheese on Hanukkah for that reason (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 670:2). Some medieval hymns for the Sabbath of Hanukkah also tell her story, as the McClintock and Strong Cyclopaedia notes. These are later Jewish uses of the story, not evidence that Jews counted the book as Scripture.

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
Judith is full of the books of the Hebrew Bible, and these links run from the Hebrew Bible to Judith, not the other way.

  • Judges 4–5: Jael kills Sisera in her tent, and Deborah sings, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24). Judith 13:18 echoes the blessing.
  • Exodus 15: the song at the sea and Miriam leading the women with drums (Exodus 15:20–21), the model for Judith's song and dance (15:12–16:17). "The Lord is a God who shatters wars" (16:2) takes up the Greek of Exodus 15:3.
  • Genesis 34: Simeon's revenge for Dinah, which Judith praises in her prayer (9:2–4), though Jacob condemns it (Genesis 49:5–7).
  • 1 Samuel 17: one weak fighter, a giant's head brought back and his army routed.
  • Deuteronomy: the teaching that Israel prospers when it obeys and suffers when it sins, which Achior summarizes (5:17–21), and the command not to put God to the test (8:12; Deuteronomy 6:16).
  • Exodus 17 and Numbers 20: a people dying of thirst who grumble against their leaders (7:19–29).
  • Isaiah 66:24: fire and worm for God's enemies, at the end of Judith's song (16:17).
  • Esther and Daniel: a Jew in a foreign court who saves the people (Esther 4–7) and keeps the food laws (12:1–4; Daniel 1:8), as Esther does only in the Greek additions (Addition C).

provenance.h: How Jews and Christians first used it
provenance.b: No Jewish writer of the time quotes Judith, Josephus does not mention it, and the rabbis of the Talmud never name it. The first sure use anywhere is Christian: 1 Clement 55.4–5 (about AD 96), written from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, holds up "the blessed Judith" beside Esther as women who risked themselves for their people. Clement does not quote the book as Scripture, but he assumes his readers know the story. Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and Origen mention or cite it in the 200s, and Jerome's preface praises her as a model of chastity for men and women alike.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible has 24 books (the Christian Old Testament's 39 counted differently), and Judith is not among them. Josephus, writing about AD 95, says the Jews have 22 books, written from Moses to the reign of Artaxerxes, after which the exact line of prophets failed (Against Apion 1.38–41). Judith is set before that, but it was written later, and Josephus, who retells much of Jewish history, never mentions it. Origen reported that the Jews did not have it even among their apocrypha in Hebrew. Jerome said they read it among the Hagiographa but did not use it to settle disputed questions. Protestants argue in its strongest form, and some earlier Catholic and Orthodox teachers drew a similar line (Cardinal Cajetan, quoted by Archibald Alexander, called Judith insufficient to prove any matter of faith; Philaret's catechism notes that such books are not in the Hebrew): the Old Testament was entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2), Jesus and the apostles used Israel's Scriptures, and the New Testament never quotes Judith. So the church should receive the books Israel received.

Jerome (about 347–420) made his Old Testament from the Hebrew, the Hebraica veritas, "Hebrew truth." In the preface to Samuel and Kings he named Judith among books that are not in the canon. In the preface to the books of Solomon he said the church reads Judith, Tobit and the Maccabees but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, reading them for the building up of the people, not to confirm church doctrine. It is the sentence Article VI echoes ("as Hierome saith"). Yet Jerome translated Judith at the bishops' request, and his preface to it reports that Nicaea had counted it among the Scriptures (see "What Jerome meant by Nicaea"). Athanasius and Rufinus drew a similar line, and Cyril of Jerusalem gave a 22-book list without Judith. Augustine, by contrast, counted Judith in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13), though he noted that the Jews were said not to have received it (City of God 18.26), and the North African councils followed him.

Scholars of every church note that the book's history does not fit the known record: Nebuchadnezzar ruling the Assyrians from Nineveh (1:1), a Median king unknown to history (1:1), a Persian-named general in a post-exilic Judea (2:4; 4:3), and a town no one has found. These are set out under "How reliable is it?" Archibald Alexander and other Protestant writers took them as proof that the book is not inspired history. Most Catholic and Orthodox scholars today see in them what kind of book it is, a story told to teach, which, on their view, says nothing against its inspiration.

Protestant writers from the 1500s on also objected to the book's morals, in their strongest form:

  • Lies blessed by God. Judith prays, "Strike down the slave with the ruler, and the ruler with his servant, by the deceit of my lips" (9:10; also 9:13), and then tells Holofernes a string of falsehoods while promising, "I will not tell my lord a lie tonight" (11:5). Archibald Alexander wrote that she speaks almost nothing but falsehood to Holofernes and asks the God of truth to bless deliberate deceit. The Bible forbids false witness and says God does not lie (Exodus 20:16; Titus 1:2).
  • A massacre praised. Judith thanks God for the sword he gave Simeon to avenge Dinah (9:2–4), though Jacob cursed Simeon's and Levi's anger (Genesis 49:5–7).
  • Seduction and killing. She uses her beauty to bring a man to drink and then beheads him in his bed (12:16–13:8), and the song praises her for it (16:6–9).
  • Vengeance. The McClintock and Strong Cyclopaedia (1867–1887) judged that the spirit of vengeance in the book conflicts with the teaching of both Testaments.

Luther, more gently, thought the book was best read as a poem or allegory, not as an example to copy in detail.

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b:
On the canon. Catholic and Orthodox teachers both say the church received the Old Testament in Greek from the apostles' time, the Septuagint that the New Testament writers often quote, and has read Judith since 1 Clement. Catholic teachers add that the canon was the church's to recognize, as Hippo, Carthage, Innocent I, Florence and Trent did. Orthodox teachers do not appeal to Florence or Trent, which the East did not receive; they point to the Septuagint the church has always read and to the Synod of Jerusalem (1672).

On the history. Since Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943), Catholic scholars are urged to ask what kind of writing a book is. A story told to teach can be inspired without being a chronicle (see "How reliable is it?").

On the lies. The churches that keep the book answer in two ways. Catholic moral teaching, following Augustine, holds that every lie is wrong and does not defend Judith's. Thomas Aquinas wrote that Judith is praised not for lying to Holofernes but for her desire to save the people, for which she put herself in danger (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 110, article 3). The Catechism defines a lie as speaking a falsehood in order to deceive (2482) and holds that lying is always wrong. On this reading, the book reports what Judith did and praises her faith and courage without approving every means, as it does with Rahab (Joshua 2:4–6; Hebrews 11:31) and the Hebrew midwives (Exodus 1:19–20). Many Greek Fathers did not hold Augustine's absolute rule. John Chrysostom defended deceit used for a good end, saying that its value is great "provided it be not introduced with a mischievous intention," and praised generals who won by stratagem (On the Priesthood 1.8). John Cassian, who brought the teaching of the Egyptian monks to the West, compared a lie to hellebore, a dangerous medicine to be used only in grave danger, and approved Rahab's and Hushai's deceptions (Conferences 17.17–19). Neither discusses Judith, but on their principle her ruse can be read as a stratagem of war against an aggressor rather than the sin of lying; we have found no Orthodox ruling on Judith herself. Readers in both traditions also note that much of what Judith says is true in a double sense (11:5–6, 16–19), so that the deceit lies partly in Holofernes' own desire.

On the killing. The book itself invites the comparison with Jael (13:18 echoes Judges 5:24), and those who defend it point to Jael (Judges 4:21; Judges 5:24–27) and Ehud (Judges 3:15–23), whom the Hebrew Bible honors for killing an oppressor of Israel, and David's beheading of Goliath (1 Samuel 17:51). Judith kills a commander leading a war to destroy her people and their Temple, not a private enemy; she keeps herself pure (13:16), and she gives the glory to God (13:14–15; 16:5–6).

cited_in.b: Elizabeth to Mary: "You are blessed among women" (Greek eulogēmenē sy en gynaixin). Uzziah says to Judith, "Daughter, you are blessed by God Most High above all the women on earth!" (13:18), and Achior later says, "Blessed are you in every tent of Judah" (14:7, with the same Greek form eulogēmenē sy as Luke). But the phrase goes back to Deborah's blessing of Jael, "Blessed above women be Jael" (Judges 5:24), whose Greek (in the Vaticanus text) has en gynaixin, "among women," as Luke does. Luke, Judith and Judges share a way of blessing a woman through whom God strikes Israel's enemy or brings salvation. Catholic tradition hears Judith in Elizabeth's words, and the liturgy applies 13:18 to Mary. A direct borrowing from Judith cannot be shown, since Judges 5:24 explains Luke's wording as well. In the Byzantine text and the KJV, Gabriel says the same words at Luke 1:28 ("blessed art thou among women"), which is where many readers know them.

Mary's song praises God who scatters the proud, brings down rulers and lifts up the lowly (Luke 1:51–53), and who has looked on the lowliness (tapeinōsis) of his servant (Luke 1:48). In Judith the people pray God to "have pity on the low state of our people" (6:19) and wait "in great distress" (7:32, Greek en tapeinōsei, the same noun); Judith prays to "the God of the lowly" (tapeinoi), "the helper of the least, the protector of the weak" (9:11); Uzziah blesses her for not holding back her life when the people were humbled (13:20); and her song praises God who brought the enemy to nothing "by a woman's hand" (16:5–7). Both songs draw on Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and on Exodus 15, so the link is a shared tradition of women's victory songs, not a quotation.

Anna the prophet, a widow of great age, who never left the Temple and served God "with fasting and prayer night and day" (Luke 2:37). Judith is a widow who fasts (8:4–6), tells Holofernes, "Night and day she serves the God of heaven" (11:17), and lives to 105 (16:23). Luke 2:37 can be read either as "until she was eighty-four" or as "a widow for eighty-four years"; some scholars, such as I. Howard Marshall and J. K. Elliott, prefer the second, which would make Anna, married young and wed for seven years, about 105, Judith's age at death. If Luke's numbers are read that way, the likeness may be deliberate. Whether Luke had Judith in mind is still unknown, since devout widows who fast and pray were a familiar Jewish ideal (compare 1 Timothy 5:5).

Paul says the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God, and that no one knows a person's thoughts except that person's own spirit. Judith tells the elders, "You cannot find the bottom of a human heart... How will you search out God?" (8:14). Both use the Greek words for "depth" (bathos, "bottom" in the Plain) and "search" (ereunaō) and move from the human heart to God. Hugh Pope in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) argued that Paul seems to quote the Greek of Judith here. Most commentators see only a likeness of idea, common in Jewish wisdom (Job 11:7; Proverbs 20:27; Isaiah 40:13), with Paul's point the opposite of Judith's: God's depths cannot be searched by us, but the Spirit reveals them. Paul's later cry, "how unsearchable his judgments" (Romans 11:33–34), quoting Isaiah 40:13, belongs to the same tradition. Disputed.

Those who by faith "were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight," and women who received their dead raised. Readers sometimes ask whether Judith is meant, since she was made strong in weakness and routed a foreign army. Most commentators connect 11:34–38 instead with the Maccabees, and 11:35 with the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, and with Gideon, David and the judges (Hebrews 11:32). A link to Judith is possible but not generally held.

Stephen's and Paul's speeches retell Israel's history from Abraham's call out of Mesopotamia (Acts 7:2–4) through Egypt and the exodus to the land, to show what God has done. Achior gives Holofernes the same kind of summary, from the ancestors' departure from Chaldea (5:6–9) through Egypt (5:10–12), the wilderness and the conquest (5:13–16), to sin, exile and return (5:17–19). Both follow the pattern of Joshua 24:2–13, Nehemiah 9:6–37 and Psalm 105. Shared form; Acts does not depend on Judith.

Jesus praises the Father as "Lord of heaven and earth." Judith calls God "Master of heaven and earth" (9:12; Greek despota tōn ouranōn kai tēs gēs). A common Jewish form of address in prayer (Genesis 14:19; Tobit 7:17 in the shorter Greek); a shared tradition, not a borrowing.

"Where their worm does not die and the fire is not put out" (Mark 9:48). Judith's song ends with God punishing the nations that rise against Israel "on the day of judgment": "He will put fire and worms into their flesh, and they will weep and feel it forever" (16:17). The weeping recalls Jesus' sayings about weeping and grinding of teeth (Matthew 24:51; Matthew 8:12), and the unending pain recalls Revelation 14:10–11. All of these take up the last verse of Isaiah (Isaiah 66:24), and Sirach 7:17 has the same pairing of fire and worms. Judith is an early witness to reading Isaiah's picture as judgment that lasts forever; the New Testament passages draw on the same tradition.

The Lord disciplines those he loves, and suffering is training. Judith tells the elders that the Lord whips those who come near him, to warn them, and has not taken vengeance on them (8:27), and that he tests his people as he tested Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:25–26). Both draw on Proverbs 3:11–12 (also James 1:2–3; 1 Peter 1:6–7). Shared tradition.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish faith in the last two centuries before Jesus, Judith is valuable: it shows how a people that had lived through the Maccabean crisis prayed, fasted, kept the food laws and trusted God against an empire, and how it imagined a heroine. As a text, it survived well in Greek, in the great codices and many later manuscripts that differ in detail, but its Semitic original is lost, and Jerome's Latin, made from a different Aramaic copy, is shorter and free. As history, its setting cannot stand: Nebuchadnezzar never ruled the Assyrians from Nineveh, Arphaxad is unknown, the Jews had not yet returned from exile under Nebuchadnezzar, and Bethulia has never been found. Most scholars, including most Catholic scholars since the mid-1900s, read it as a deliberately unhistorical story told to teach. Catholic teaching on literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu; Dei Verbum 12) leaves room for that, and the Church has made no ruling on its genre, while older Catholic readers, and some readers today, defend its history. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their faith in the one God who saves the lowly, closely follows Israel's stories of deliverance, and in its heroine's lies and violence raises moral questions on which the churches answer differently.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before Jesus: high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. Written most likely in the generation after the Maccabees, Judith shows the piety of Judean Jews of that time: public fasting and sackcloth before the altar (4:9–15), prayer at the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem (9:1), a widow's ascetic life of fasting except on Sabbaths and feasts (8:6), the food laws kept strictly in a Gentile camp (12:1–4), ritual bathing before prayer (12:7–9), the high priest and council ruling from Jerusalem (4:6–8; 15:8), and the conversion of a Gentile by circumcision (14:10). It shows how the stories of Jael, Deborah, Miriam and David were read and retold, and the hope that God defends his Temple. It is also a window on how Jews of the time imagined a woman's courage and holiness. The lack of any copy at Qumran, and of any Jewish quotation before the Middle Ages, means we know less about who read it than for Tobit or 1 Enoch.

Good in Greek, lost in the original. The Greek is preserved in Codex Vaticanus, Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus (300s–400s AD) and in groups of later manuscripts, which differ in many small ways but tell the same story with the same speeches. The Old Latin and Syriac were made from the Greek. Jerome's Vulgate was made in one night, by his own account, from an Aramaic copy, and he says he cut out the many faulty variants he found; it is about a fifth shorter, with its own additions. The Hebrew or Aramaic original does not survive, no ancient Semitic fragment has been found, and the medieval Hebrew versions are later retellings. So the Greek is our earliest text, and for passages where it seems to misread the Hebrew, the original can only be guessed.

The book dates its events to Nebuchadnezzar's twelfth and eighteenth years (1:1; 2:1), soon after the Jews returned from exile (4:3). The details do not fit what is known:

  • Nebuchadnezzar, "who ruled over the Assyrians in Nineveh" (1:1). Nebuchadnezzar II was king of Babylon (605–562 BC). Nineveh had been destroyed in 612 BC by the Babylonians and Medes, before his reign, and the Assyrian empire was gone. Ancient readers who knew Kings, Jeremiah and Daniel could not have missed this; most scholars think it is on purpose, joining Israel's two great destroyers into one.
  • Arphaxad, king of the Medes (1:1–15). No king of that name is known. The Ecbatana he builds, with its huge walls (1:2–4), recalls Herodotus's account of the city of the Median king Deioces (Histories 1.98). Older Catholic scholars identified Arphaxad with Phraortes or another Median king; most scholars see an invented figure, perhaps named after Arpachshad of Genesis 10:22.
  • The time after the exile. The Jews "had only lately come up from captivity" and the Temple had been consecrated again (4:3; 5:18–19). The return from Babylon came under Cyrus of Persia in 538 BC and the Temple was rebuilt in 520–515 BC (Ezra 1; Ezra 6:15), long after Nebuchadnezzar's death. The high priest Joakim (4:6) shares his name with Joiakim, high priest after the return (Nehemiah 12:10, 26).
  • Persian names. The general Holofernes and the eunuch Bagoas (12:11) bear Persian names, and both are known from the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes III: a Cappadocian prince Holofernes fought in Egypt for him (Diodorus 31.19, dated 352 BC by the Encyclopaedia Judaica), and the eunuch Bagoas led his reconquest of Egypt in 343 BC (Diodorus 16.47–50). Hugh Pope already noted the book's "Persian and even a Greek colouring."
  • Bethulia. This town, with its springs, passes and view of Esdraelon and Dothan (4:6; 6:11; 7:3), is central to the story but appears nowhere else, and no site has been agreed. Scholars have proposed several towns in Samaria, including Shechem, or read the name as a symbol ("virgin," or "house of God"). Some of the other places in 1–2 and 4 are also unknown.
  • The march of Holofernes' army (2:21–28) covers impossible distances in a few days.

The Catholic answer. Older Catholic scholars defended the history: Hugh Pope's Catholic Encyclopedia article (1910) reports Calmet's identification of Arphaxad with Phraortes and Vigouroux's of Nebuchadnezzar with Ashurbanipal, and puts the errors of names and places down to translators and copyists. Since Pius XII's encyclical Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943), Catholic interpreters are urged to identify the literary forms the biblical writers used, and the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (11–12) teaches that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation, expressed differently in history, prophecy, poetry and other forms. On that basis most Catholic scholars today read Judith as a story told to teach, with names and dates chosen for their meaning. The Orthodox answer. The Orthodox churches have made no ruling known to us. They read the book for its moral and spiritual teaching, and many Orthodox teachers already give these books a different rank from the Hebrew canon. The critical view. Most scholars of every background see a deliberately unhistorical story whose first readers were meant to recognize the mixture of eras. A fair summary: the evidence rules out reading the setting as accurate history; whether that matters for the book's authority depends on what kind of book a church thinks it is.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: the one God who alone is God, against a king who claims worship (3:8; 6:2; 16:13–15; Daniel 3; Isaiah 45:5); God's strength not in numbers but with the lowly (9:11; 1 Samuel 17:47; Psalm 33:16–18; Zechariah 4:6); trust without testing God (8:11–17; Deuteronomy 6:16); God's discipline as warning (8:27; Proverbs 3:11–12); repentance, prayer and fasting in danger (4:9–15; Joel 2:12–17); keeping the food laws among Gentiles (12:1–4; Daniel 1:8); the Gentile who comes to believe (14:10; Ruth 1:16; Isaiah 56:6–7).
  • Goes beyond: a woman as Israel's sole deliverer in a whole book of her own; a stricter piety of continual fasting and widowhood (8:6; 16:22) than the Torah requires.
  • Differs or may conflict: (a) Judith's deception, which she asks God to bless (9:10, 13; 11:5–19). Protestant writers see a conflict with the command against false witness and with God who does not lie (Exodus 20:16; Proverbs 12:22; Titus 1:2). Catholic teaching agrees that lying is wrong and reads Scripture as praising her faith and courage, not the lie (Aquinas). (b) Praise of Simeon's massacre (9:2–4) against Jacob's curse (Genesis 49:5–7): the prayer praises God's punishment of the rape of Dinah, which Genesis also condemns (Genesis 34:7), while Genesis 49 condemns the brothers' violence. (c) Achior's conversion (14:10) conflicts with the letter of Deuteronomy 23:3, which bars Ammonites from the assembly. The strongest rabbinic answer is the Mishnah's ruling that an Ammonite convert named Judah could enter, because Sennacherib had mixed up the nations (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4); the chapter pages discuss it. (d) Violence and revenge (13:8; 16:17): Jael and Ehud are precedents in the Hebrew Bible; critics see a spirit of vengeance at odds with Jesus' teaching (Matthew 5:43–45). (e) The historical setting (section 3).
  • Each church's view: Catholic and Orthodox churches read Judith as Scripture in harmony with the rest of the Bible and with the church's moral teaching, so they read (a) to (d) in the ways given above, though on (a) they give different reasons (see "How the churches that keep it answer"). Lutheran and Anglican churches read it as a good human book, useful for its example of faith and courage, to be tested by the canonical books and never used to establish doctrine. Reformed, Baptist and most evangelical churches see points (a), (b) and (e) as signs that the book is not inspired, while valuing it as a window on Jewish faith before Christ.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Judith is in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to it. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, though Lutheran and Anglican tradition commends it for example of life, and every reader can learn from it how Jews of the Maccabean age prayed and hoped. Either way, read it with respect and with an eye to the differences on this page.

Check the introduction of your Bible. Most modern Catholic, Orthodox and ecumenical Bibles translate the Greek; the Douay-Rheims translates Jerome's shorter Vulgate, with different verse numbers (the Greek 13:18 is Vulgate 13:23, and 15:9–10 is Vulgate 15:10–11) and some lines of its own. The King James Apocrypha translates the Greek. A verse you remember from a hymn or the Mass may come from the Vulgate.

how_to_read.h: Read it as a story with irony
how_to_read.b: Do not start by asking which Nebuchadnezzar it means. Start by asking why the writer gave the enemy that name, and why a widow from a town no one can find should save Israel when the army and the elders could not. Watch the two halves: chapters 1–7 build the threat, and chapters 8–16 overturn it. Watch Judith's double speech to Holofernes (11:5–19), the prayers at each turning point (4:9–15; 9; 13:4–7; 16), and the phrase "by a woman's hand" (9:10; 13:15; 16:5).

Read Judges 4–5 before Judith 12–13, Exodus 15 before Judith 16, Genesis 34 before Judith 9, and 1 Samuel 17 before Judith 13–14. Then read Luke 1:39–55 after Judith 13 and 16. You will see how Judith takes up the Hebrew Bible and how its song and blessing belong to a tradition the New Testament also uses, and you can judge for yourself where it agrees, goes beyond, or differs.

On Judith's lies and on the killing, the churches give real answers, set out above and on the chapter pages. Read each in its strongest form before deciding. Many Protestant readers find the story easier to read once they see how the Hebrew Bible itself treats Jael, Ehud and Rahab; many Catholic readers find Aquinas's distinction between praising the faith and approving the lie a help.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "Judith, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say which text you quote (Greek or Vulgate). It is one of the best backgrounds for the faith and hopes of the Maccabean age, for Jewish women's piety and for the Magnificat's song of the lowly lifted up, and a key to much of Western art.
